title: ChEA-KG and ChEA-KG-TS: a network-based transcription factor enrichment analysis tool with an accompanying time-series workflow.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped all three released networks from the site's download page (node-draw filtered 9.4 MB, target-set-swap 8.4 MB, unfiltered 13.7 MB) plus the four gene-set (GMT) atlas files, and loaded the edge and node tables in pandas. Confirmed columns (source, relation, target, z_score, p_value, source_label, target_label), zero missing values, zero duplicate source-target pairs, 549 self-loops (a transcription factor listed as regulating itself), 0 pairs appearing as both 'upregulates' and 'downregulates', all p-values below 0.01, and counts 67,650 up + 63,531 down = 131,181 edges over 1,559 nodes, exactly the paper's figure. Also opened the supplementary workbook (Supplementary Tables S1-S6) and read the methods and discussion in the open-access full text.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: How the edges were made (ChEA3 transcription-factor enrichment run on RummaGEO differential-expression gene sets, top-10 enriched factors kept, edge counts under 10 discarded, then a shuffled-network significance filter) is described only in the methods; the raw per-edge observation count is not in any downloaded file. The overlap figures with curated/experimental references (TRRUST 0.27% of directed edges, ENCODE ChIP-seq 0.95%) come from Supplementary Table S3, not from my own recomputation.

a1_downloadable.note: Verified: all nine files on https://chea-kg.maayanlab.cloud/download_files fetched anonymously from public S3 with no login; sizes matched the listed sizes.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Weak pass, verified in files: the sign ('upregulates'/'downregulates') is a column, but edge existence has only positives, so the negative class must be built as the complement of ~1.0M possible source-target pairs (one line of pandas, open-world assumption).

a3_inputs_present.note: Verified: nodes carry only NCBI gene ID and gene symbol, no sequences; fetching protein sequences or promoter DNA for 1,559 transcription factors is a small, routine lookup, not thousands of ambiguous ones.

a4_units_stated.note: Verified: the only numeric columns are z_score and p_value, both dimensionless statistics defined in the methods; no data dictionary ships with the download, but nothing is unit-ambiguous.

a5_enough_rows.note: Verified by counting: 67,650 'upregulates' + 63,531 'downregulates' edges across 1,559 nodes (655-700 distinct source factors).

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~24 MB of CSV from a 9.4 MB zip
a6_fits_laptop.note: Verified: loads into pandas in seconds, far under 16 GB RAM; no GPU needed for a link-prediction baseline at this scale.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Verified exactly: 131,181 edges / 1,559 nodes in the node-draw file, 109,813 in target-set-swap, 373,250 unfiltered - all three match the paper and the site's manifest.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL. Every edge is the output of ChEA3, an enrichment tool whose own output the authors' Supplementary Table S1 calls a 'ranked list of TFs predicted to regulate' a gene set: an edge exists when a factor fell in ChEA3's top 10 for at least 10 gene sets. ChEA3 ranks factors by aggregating ChIP-seq libraries and co-expression libraries (ARCHS4, GTEx), so a predictor using sequence, binding or co-expression features would be re-deriving its own label, and the z_score/p_value columns are computed from the same edge counts rather than from any independent measurement. The authors' own benchmark finds only 0.27% of directed edges in TRRUST (curated literature) and 0.95% in ENCODE ChIP-seq, and the discussion concedes that confirming these 'inferred regulatory relationships' would require knockdown or overexpression experiments nobody has done. Training on these edges distills ChEA3, not biology.

existing_models.name: ChEA-KG itself (this paper's network-construction pipeline: ChEA3 enrichment over RummaGEO gene sets plus a shuffling-based edge filter)
existing_models.score_and_split: No held-out predictive metric is reported; evaluation is overlap of its 131,181 edges with eight reference libraries (Supplementary Table S3): 0.27% of directed edges in TRRUST versus 0.1% expected by chance, 0.95% in ENCODE ChIP-seq versus 1.1% expected.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The discussion states that testing against other sources of known factor-factor interactions would strengthen confidence and that only in vitro/in vivo knockdown, knockout or overexpression would confirm the inferred links.

existing_models.name: GRINCD, a causal-discovery plus graph-neural-network method for regulatory links
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported as superior or comparable to correlation-based methods, and explicitly covers transcription-factor-to-transcription-factor pairs, which is exactly this network's content; split details not retrieved.

existing_models.name: GNNLink and GENELink, graph-neural-network link predictors for regulatory edges
existing_models.score_and_split: GNNLink reported best on 41 of 44 benchmark datasets by precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC), at least 4% above GENELink on ~41% of them; benchmarks are the standard single-cell sets with curated ground-truth networks.

existing_models.name: GRNFormer, a graph-transformer regulatory-network inference model (Bioinformatics 2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Average sampled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and sampled PR-AUC between 0.90 and 0.98 - note 'sampled' negatives, which is a generous split.

existing_models.name: scRegNet, single-cell foundation models joined to graph learning for regulatory link prediction
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported state of the art on seven single-cell RNA-sequencing benchmarks, each with four ground-truth networks.

existing_models.name: BEELINE, the standard benchmarking framework for regulatory-network inference (Nature Methods 2020)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not a model but the accepted evaluation harness; found that methods needing no pseudotime (GENIE3, GRNBoost2, PIDC) performed best on curated models.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Inference accuracy on curated networks remains low overall.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model) for transcription-factor sequences, or DNABERT-2 / Nucleotide Transformer for target promoters
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU: 1,559 protein embeddings from the small ESM-2 checkpoint is roughly an hour
backbone.licence: ESM-2 MIT; the ChEA-KG article and site are CC BY-NC (non-commercial), the web interface code is GPL-3.0

integration.partner_dataset: ReMap / ENCODE ChIP-seq peaks, TRRUST, and the Human Transcription Factor database, joinable on NCBI gene ID already present in the node file
integration.join_key: NCBI Gene ID (present as the 'id' column and in the node URI)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which of the 131,181 inferred factor-to-factor edges are corroborated by independent physical binding evidence - but ChEA3 already consumes ReMap and ENCODE to build these edges, so the partner data is upstream of the label rather than independent of it.

controls.positive_control: Known autoregulatory and textbook pairs (for example MYC-MAX family links) should score highest; 549 self-loops exist in the file and are construction artifacts rather than controls.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle edge signs and confirm collapse; also fit on node degree alone, since source out-degree ranges to 354 and would likely carry most of the signal.
controls.external_validation: TRRUST curated edges - but only 0.27% of directed ChEA-KG edges are in TRRUST, so it cannot serve as an agreeing reference.

honest_claim_h3: A model trained on this network would claim only: 'I can reproduce which transcription factors the ChEA3 enrichment tool ranks in its top ten for RummaGEO gene sets', not that any predicted regulatory relationship exists in a cell.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use transcription factor sequence and network context to predict which factor switches another factor's gene on or off.
plain_idea.train_on: 131,181 verified rows, each a pair of human transcription factors (proteins that switch genes on or off) with a direction and an up/down sign, over 1,559 factors; features would be protein-language-model embeddings plus network context.
plain_idea.predict: Whether factor A regulates factor B and in which direction. The true answer here is not a measurement: it is the output of the ChEA3 enrichment tool applied to public differential-expression gene sets, filtered against shuffled networks.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Regulatory-network maps guide which factor a lab perturbs next, so a model that filled in missing edges would be used - but only if the training edges were real measurements, which these are not.

more_or_better_data.why: 1,559 factors beats TRRUST's 800 and most single-cell benchmarks' 500-1,000 genes, and the signed direction (up versus down) is rarer than plain directed edges; but the extra size comes from algorithmic inference, not extra measurement.

confidence_score.why: The per-edge z_score and p_value are computed against shuffled networks from the same counts, so they measure how often ChEA3 said it, not measurement noise; no replicate experiments exist and the raw count column is not even in the download.

models_beatable.why: GNNLink, GRNFormer (2026) and scRegNet are recent graph-neural and foundation-model methods reporting 0.90-0.98 AUROC on the established BEELINE-style benchmarks; competing on a different, unvalidated label set would not be comparable to them.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first and third conditions: no existing model is trained on this label, and the obvious partner data (ReMap/ENCODE ChIP-seq) was already consumed by ChEA3 to generate these very edges, so adding it leaks rather than improves.

ml_idea: Considered: link prediction over the released signed, directed transcription-factor network - given two human transcription factors, predict whether one upregulates or downregulates the other, from ESM-2 protein embeddings plus promoter-sequence and graph-topology features, with factors held out so test pairs involve unseen regulators. Rejected on label provenance. The only reframings that survive turn the network into a feature table for an externally measured outcome (for example gene dependency in DepMap, or mouse knockout phenotypes), where the unit count drops to ~1,559 factors and this paper contributes one feature block among many.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed end to end: I did load all three networks in pandas in seconds, so the 24 MB working set and ~2 GB peak RAM (dominated by a ~1M-row negative-pair frame) are safe; the embedding hour assumes the small ESM-2 checkpoint on 1,559 sequences at roughly 0.5 sequences per second on CPU.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read how the edges were made, then look at Supplementary Table S3: 0.27% overlap with TRRUST and 0.95% with ENCODE ChIP-seq tells you the labels are not corroborated measurements. Thirty minutes, and it kills the project before any download.

verdict_reason: Fails A8 (label provenance). The 131,181 edges are not measurements: each one exists because the ChEA3 enrichment tool ranked a transcription factor in its top ten for at least ten public gene sets, and ChEA3 builds those rankings from the same ChIP-seq and co-expression libraries a model would use as features - so the project would distill ChEA3 and inherit its unknown error profile. The authors' own benchmark finds only 0.27% of directed edges in curated TRRUST and 0.95% in ENCODE ChIP-seq, and their discussion concedes the links are unconfirmed pending knockdown or overexpression experiments. Everything else is exemplary: the files download without a login, the counts match the paper exactly (67,650 + 63,531 = 131,181 over 1,559 nodes), there are no duplicates, no missing values and no sign conflicts, and it all fits in 24 MB - which is why the failure is worth recording precisely.
